topics.title: A Revenue Layer for CKB Nodes

recent_posts.topic_title: A Revenue Layer for CKB Nodes
recent_posts.author: psawyerberlin
recent_posts.content_html:
Thanks all. Answering the last three together. I’m also updating the first post to reflect where this thread has taken the idea. Corrected parts are struck through, not deleted, so the history stays visible.

Where this came from. The trigger was a concrete need: CRT needs many independent nodes to hold key shares and release them when the conditions are met. Rather than recruit a separate network just for CRT, I asked whether CKB node operators could run it. The idea is generic: the same runner could host CRT, CrowdCell’s finalization bot, and any app that today depends on one server of its own.

@janx Agreed, a separate project. A tool that runs beside the node, never inside ckb. CKBadger can stay what it is; at most, its data could be read, not extended.

@Ayoub_Lesfer That’s exactly the use case, thanks. Permissionless release/refund plus a fee already paid from the pledge cell means a runner needs no funds and no trust. A small keeper tip in the lock script is all that’s missing, paid to whoever submits the transaction first. When there’s a testnet version, CrowdCell and CRT would be the two pilots. What tip would feel reasonable to your users?

@NightLantern Fair points, and I agree with several of them:

  1. Not broken: agreed. Unpaid verification works, and this doesn’t try to fix it. The revenue is a by-product (see #14); the goal is apps that don’t depend on a single server.
  2. Cost for apps: it adds no cost to apps that don’t use it. Apps that do run a bot or keeper already pay for it today (a server, an operator, a single point of failure). The runner replaces that cost; it doesn’t add one. In CrowdCell’s case the tip would come from the pledge cell, just as the fee already does.
  3. What’s incentivized: on PoW, consensus is hashpower, not node count, so “consensus threshold” was the wrong word in my first post. But I still think more independent nodes make things safer. For a service like CRT, more nodes holding shares means more operators would have to collude to break it. For the network, more full nodes mean more independent verification and a network that’s harder to isolate or censor. The key word is independent, which is why pay is per job done, not per node (ten idle nodes earn nothing), and why node choice would rely on reputation and diversity, not node count.
  4. Mining: agreed. It doesn’t add hashpower or fund security. It’s a separate business beside the node, which is exactly what it should be.

So in one line: an optional side application next to a full node, which earns only once many apps use it as their decentralised backend.

recent_posts.topic_title: A Revenue Layer for CKB Nodes
recent_posts.author: psawyerberlin
recent_posts.content_text:
The project is now CKB Service Runner: a separate application you install next to your full node. It needs no change to ckb and no consensus change, and nothing runs unless the operator opts in.
github.com
GitHub - psawyerberlin/ckb-service-runner: Side application for CKB full nodes: dashboard,...
Side application for CKB full nodes: dashboard, node ranking, and a sandboxed service runtime
The plan, in two phases (testnet first):
Phase 1: dashboard and node ranking. A web dashboard for your node (based on a CKB fork of mempool) and a public ranking of runner nodes by availability, sync, age and network diversity, summarised weekly in a stat cell. Operators get something useful from day one, before any paying service exists.
Phase 2: service runtime. Once the network has run for 12 months with at least 60 diverse nodes, services published as cells run in a CKB-VM sandbox. CRT (revocable timelock) would be the first.

recent_posts.topic_title: A Revenue Layer for CKB Nodes
recent_posts.author: Ayoub_Lesfer
recent_posts.content_text: @psawyerberlin sounds good, happy to be one of the two pilots. On the tip: the pledge lock already caps what can leave a pledge cell at 1 CKB on release or refund, and the minimum pledge is 100 CKB, so I’d keep the tip inside that cap. Flat per pledge cell, not a percentage, since the work is the same whatever the pledge size. That’s under 1% on the smallest pledge and the real tx fee is a tiny part of it. On a refund it comes out of the backer’s own money, so I’d rather keep it small there. Does a flat amount per job work for the runner or do you need it to scale with something?

topics.title: 分享一个 Tinder 版预测市场应用的想法

recent_posts.topic_title: 分享一个 Tinder 版预测市场应用的想法
recent_posts.author: ArthurZhang
recent_posts.content_text:
Hi Fisher,
I think this is technically feasible now.
With CKB handling the market state / settlement and Fiber providing the micropayment layer, most of the primitives needed for this kind of high-frequency, small-value interaction are already there.
The bigger issue, in my view, is no longer implementation but liquidity bootstrapping, especially the initial LP depth for each market. A Tinder-like UX potentially creates a very large number of small markets, so liquidity can become fragmented very quickly. Even if the protocol has reasonable total TVL, each individual card may still be too shallow to provide a meaningful price or smooth entry/exit.
This can partly be avoided with pari-mutuel or peer-matching designs, but if we want Polymarket-like instant execution and continuous pricing, somebody still needs to seed the markets.

topics.title: Lineage: working through batch release evidence with CellScript

recent_posts.topic_title: Lineage: working through batch release evidence with CellScript
recent_posts.author: ArthurZhang
recent_posts.content_text:
I started building this after discussing the idea with a mate who works in pharma. As the author of CellScript, I kept coming back to the same question:
When a batch becomes “released,” what exactly did someone approve—and can another participant check it without asking the original application for its verdict?
I built Lineage to work through that question. It follows a batch through evidence collection, quality review, release, and a later correction. There is a working interface, signed records, an export you can verify offline, and a release predicate executed locally in CKB-VM through CellScript.
Lineage workspace1440×1000 125 KB
These screenshots come from the browser acceptance run. The organizations, people, samples, and reports are explicitly synthetic. The uploaded bytes, signatures, VM execution, and rejected operations are real. A fresh installation starts empty.
In an autologous cell therapy, the starting cells come from the patient who will receive the treatment. A sponsor, contract manufacturer, testing lab, logistics provider, and hospital may each hold part of the record. Chain of identity concerns whose material it is; chain of custody concerns who had it.
I am interested in the handoff between existing systems: which report version was relied on, which process applied, who assessed the evidence, and what happens if a record changes after approval.
A quality owner approves a versioned policy. A batch binds to that policy, a sample reference, and a process version. Lab and manufacturing members upload files and sign declarations covering identity, potency, sterility, viability, manufacturing, and deviations.
The distinction I care about is ready for review versus approved for release. Having all the required records does not make the quality decision for you.
Complete evidence awaiting review1440×1000 112 KB
All six required declarations are present. The batch still needs an accountable approval.
Each declaration binds the exact document hash to the batch, sample, process, policy, category, assessment, and issuer. At approval, the server checks the active evidence, issuer permissions, holds, and revision. It executes the CellScript predicate, then checks again before committing the decision.
The predicate itself is intentionally small:
required evidence is present
AND required assessments pass
AND required declarations pass attribution checks
AND no hold is active
AND the batch revision still matches
The signed release records the evidence manifest, policy, revision, approver, and execution receipt. That gives the later reader a specific decision to inspect.
Released batch with its evidence commitment1440×1000 112 KB
The next part matters more to me than the green badge. Export the source bytes, declarations, policy, approvals, and signed history, then verify them locally in the browser or Node CLI. Browser verification uses Web Crypto without uploading the package. The acceptance test exercises it offline.
Export verified locally1440×1000 103 KB
Verification checks the records inside the package. The public trust directory still needs to be authenticated independently.
Changing the exported evidence produces a rejection:
Modified evidence rejected1440×1000 101 KB
I also wanted to follow the uncomfortable case. A report used in a release is later revoked. The batch goes on hold. Resolving the hold returns it to evidence collection; replacement evidence needs another approval. The earlier release remains in the history, with the evidence it originally relied on.
Revocation puts the batch on hold1440×1000 107 KB
Both release decisions remain inspectable1440×1000 110 KB
The verifier reconstructs the exported batch state from signed events and checks retained approvals against their own manifests. A valid old export remains a snapshot: it cannot tell you that no revocation happened after it was created.
Source and running instructions: GitHub - CellScript-Labs/lineage: Therapeutic batch release evidence, independent verification, and local CellScript CKB-VM checks · GitHub

topics.title: CKB Script Port: testing state transfer between light clients

recent_posts.topic_title: CKB Script Port: testing state transfer between light clients
recent_posts.author: Ticoworld
recent_posts.content_text:
I’ve been working on a small experiment called CKB Script Port.
The idea is to see whether already-synced state for one CKB Script can be moved from one light-client installation to another, so the new installation does not always have to rebuild the same Script history from scratch.
I first tested this with Pocket Node, and later with iBytes.
While testing the iBytes setup, I ran into an interesting light-client case.
A Script can be synced up to a certain block height even when the light-client database does not have the exact block hash for that height stored locally.
That matters for Script Port because if I want another light client to continue from that point, I need a boundary I can actually verify. I didn’t want to solve that by simply trusting a hash from an external RPC.
So I tested using the light client’s existing block-proof verification path to verify that historical block instead.
That worked, and I was able to complete the handoff on the iBytes setup and continue syncing from the next block.
The Script Port repo is here:
github.com
GitHub - Ticoworld/ckb-script-port
Contribute to Ticoworld/ckb-script-port development by creating an account on GitHub.
The historical-header part also became an upstream ckb-light-client contribution:
github.com/nervosnetwork/ckb-light-client
Add proof-backed historical header requests (#297)
develop ← Ticoworld:verified-historical-header-lookup-v2
opened 07:50AM - 02 Oct 26 UTC
Ticoworld
+1360
-47
## Summary
Adds an API to verify a historical block header using the light cl…ient's existing block-proof verification path.
A caller provides a block number and candidate header hash. The light client verifies that candidate against the chain state it currently accepts before reporting the request as verified.
Historical requests are tracked separately from ordinary `fetch_header` requests, so they do not change existing fetch behavior.
## Motivation
A caller may already know a historical header hash but still need the light client to verify that it belongs to the accepted chain.
Using `fetch_header(hash)` alone is not enough for this use case because a header may already exist in local cache from earlier work.
This change lets callers explicitly request fresh proof-backed verification of a historical `(block number, hash)` pair.
## Related work
PR [#292](https://github.com/nervosnetwork/ckb-light-client/pull/292) adds height binding for filter-matched block hashes inside the synchronization path.
This PR uses the same existing block-proof verification machinery, but exposes a separate caller-driven historical verification request for an explicit `(block_number, candidate_hash)` pair.
Unlike the filter-sync path, a new historical request is not satisfied by a cached header alone and becomes stale if the accepted chain tip changes before completion.
## Design
- adds `request_historical_header_proof(...)`
- adds `poll_historical_header_proof(...)`
- uses the existing `GetBlocksProof` verification logic
- treats the supplied candidate hash as untrusted until proof verification succeeds
- ties verification to the accepted tip captured when the request starts
- reports the request as stale if that accepted tip changes
- does not allow a cached header alone to satisfy a new historical verification request
- keeps historical request state separate from ordinary `fetch_header` state
- uses the existing verified-header storage path
- adds no new wire protocol or storage schema
## Validation
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check`
- `make clippy`
- `make test`
Result: **145 tests passed**.
Additional tests cover:
- successful historical-header verification
- missing-header handling
- isolation from ordinary `fetch_header` requests
- mixed ordinary and historical requests
- timeout and disconnect retry
- accepted-tip changes during a request
- cached headers not satisfying a new verification request
- the full public API → scheduler → proof verification → polling path
I’m still treating Script Port as an experiment, not as something every wallet necessarily needs.
But this was one of the more interesting things I found while testing the idea, so I thought it was worth sharing.
The CKBuilder discussion is here too:
github.com/Nervos-Community-Catalyst/CKBuilder-projects
CKB Script Port: reuse already-synced Script data on a new install
opened 09:12AM - 11 Sep 26 UTC
Ticoworld
## Project Summary
CKB Script Port is a Rust library for moving already-synced …data for one CKB Script from one light-client install to another.
The idea is simple:
If one install has already processed the history for a Script, another install should not always need to repeat that same historical work from scratch.
CKB Script Port lets the already-synced Script data be exported, imported into another install, and then normal syncing can continue from the next block.
Repository:
https://github.com/Ticoworld/ckb-script-port
---
## Why I Built It
A wallet or application may already have spent time syncing the history for a Script.
If another installation needs the same Script state, it may have to rebuild that history again.
I wanted to test a narrower alternative:
> Can already-synced data for one Script be moved safely to another light-client installation without copying the whole database?
The new installation should still remain responsible for normal chain verification and future syncing.
---
## How It Works
old install
↓
export already-synced Script data
↓
portable artifact
↓
new install
↓
import
↓
continue from the next block
The current implementation works with one exact CKB Script at a time.
It moves the Script-related state and the transaction data needed by that state.
It does not move wallet keys, mnemonics, the whole light-client database, or application caches.
---
## What Works Today
The current prototype can:
- export state for one exact lock or type Script;
- include the transaction data required by that state;
- validate the exported data before import;
- import it atomically into the destination;
- work with RocksDB and SQLite;
- move state across the supported storage backends;
- continue syncing after the imported point.
The supported light-client storage layouts are deliberately pinned. I am not claiming arbitrary-version compatibility.
---
## Pocket Reference Test
I used Pocket Node as a real reference application to test whether this works outside my own fixtures.
Pocket has not requested, adopted, or endorsed this project.
The test used:
- Pocket Node v1.8.3;
- Pocket's embedded CKB light-client SQLite state;
- a real ARM64 Android device;
- one real registered lock Script;
- a fresh destination state.
The source had already processed that Script through block:
`22,370,055`
After importing the Script state, the destination's first new filter request started at:
`22,370,056`
which is the next block.
A later matching transaction was then processed normally, and the resulting state remained usable after Pocket was stopped and restarted.
As a comparison, the clean control without the imported state started filtering from the older configured historical range.
The Pocket reference evidence is here:
https://github.com/Ticoworld/ckb-script-port/blob/master/docs/G3_FINAL_REFERENCE_PRODUCT_CHECKPOINT.md
---
## What This Shows
For the tested Pocket/light-client setup, already-synced state for one Script could be moved to a fresh destination and reused instead of rebuilding that same accepted range again.
What I do not know yet is whether this is useful enough to exist as a reusable CKB component.
That is the main reason I am opening this issue now.
---
## What It Does Not Do
CKB Script Port is not:
- wallet backup or recovery;
- mnemonic or private-key migration;
- full light-client database backup;
- application-cache migration;
- proof of arbitrary historical completeness;
- arbitrary-version migration;
- multi-Script atomic migration;
- a universal performance improvement;
- a Pocket production integration.
If the original local state has already been lost, normal recovery and resync are still required.
And if somebody simply wants to clone an entire same-version installation, copying the whole database may be simpler.
The specific problem I am testing is narrower:
> Can already-synced data for one Script be reused on another install?
---
## Why I Am Asking for Feedback Now
The prototype has reached the point where I do not want to keep adding features based only on my own assumptions.
I have paused further scope expansion while I get feedback on whether this responsibility itself makes sense.
The main question is where this kind of functionality belongs, if it is useful at all:
- a separate reusable library;
- `ckb-light-client` itself;
- individual applications that need migration;
- or nowhere, because an existing mechanism already handles the problem better.
---
## Feedback I Would Appreciate
1. Is reusing already-synced Script data between light-client installations a useful problem to solve?
2. Does this make sense as a reusable library, or should applications handle it themselves?
3. Would this fit better inside `ckb-light-client`?
4. Is one exact Script per handoff a reasonable starting point?
5. Is there already a more natural CKB/light-client way to achieve the same result?
6. What evidence would you want to see next before considering this worth continuing?
I am especially interested in criticism of the boundary itself.
If this belongs somewhere else, or if existing CKB mechanisms already solve it more cleanly, I would rather find that out now before building more.
---
## Current Status
Repository:
https://github.com/Ticoworld/ckb-script-port
Development is currently paused while I collect feedback.
I am not treating the current result as proof of ecosystem demand or preparing a funding proposal from it yet.

Pocket has not requested, adopted, or endorsed this project. The test used: - Pocket Node v1.8.3; - Pocket's embedded CKB light-client SQLite state; - a real ARM64 Android device; - one real registered lock Script; - a fresh destination state. The source had already processed that Script through block: `22,370,055` After importing the Script state, the destination's first new filter request started at: `22,370,056` which is the next block. A later matching transaction was then processed normally, and the resulting state remained usable after Pocket was stopped and restarted. As a comparison, the clean control without the imported state started filtering from the older configured historical range. The Pocket reference evidence is here: https://github.com/Ticoworld/ckb-script-port/blob/master/docs/G3_FINAL_REFERENCE_PRODUCT_CHECKPOINT.md --- ## What This Shows For the tested Pocket/light-client setup, already-synced state for one Script could be moved to a fresh destination and reused instead of rebuilding that same accepted range again. What I do not know yet is whether this is useful enough to exist as a reusable CKB component. That is the main reason I am opening this issue now. --- ## What It Does Not Do CKB Script Port is not: - wallet backup or recovery; - mnemonic or private-key migration; - full light-client database backup; - application-cache migration; - proof of arbitrary historical completeness; - arbitrary-version migration; - multi-Script atomic migration; - a universal performance improvement; - a Pocket production integration. If the original local state has already been lost, normal recovery and resync are still required. And if somebody simply wants to clone an entire same-version installation, copying the whole database may be simpler. The specific problem I am testing is narrower: > Can already-synced data for one Script be reused on another install? --- ## Why I Am Asking for Feedback Now The prototype has reached the point where I do not want to keep adding features based only on my own assumptions. I have paused further scope expansion while I get feedback on whether this responsibility itself makes sense. The main question is where this kind of functionality belongs, if it is useful at all: - a separate reusable library; - `ckb-light-client` itself; - individual applications that need migration; - or nowhere, because an existing mechanism already handles the problem better. --- ## Feedback I Would Appreciate 1. Is reusing already-synced Script data between light-client installations a useful problem to solve? 2. Does this make sense as a reusable library, or should applications handle it themselves? 3. Would this fit better inside `ckb-light-client`? 4. Is one exact Script per handoff a reasonable starting point? 5. Is there already a more natural CKB/light-client way to achieve the same result? 6. What evidence would you want to see next before considering this worth continuing? I am especially interested in criticism of the boundary itself. If this belongs somewhere else, or if existing CKB mechanisms already solve it more cleanly, I would rather find that out now before building more. --- ## Current Status Repository: https://github.com/Ticoworld/ckb-script-port Development is currently paused while I collect feedback.
